extracted.intended_audience: government administrators, public administration students, and bureau managers (particularly in departments like Agriculture)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing, reviewing, and executing program planning and purchasing procedures in large public agencies, covering centralized vs decentralized planning, emergency shortcuts, plan content and review, workload classification, and stock/contract purchasing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of state plans with regional and national objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoming state plans are integrated with regional and national governmental objectives through inter-bureau committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration is done via inter-bureau committees so planning in the Department is as co-operative as in the states; results are plans for co-ordinate action of the appropriate agencies, frequently interstate in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design step: deciding who does what, when, and where
rubrics_metrics.description: Design (the fourth step in planning) means deciding who does what, when, and where; it may also be viewed as the first step in execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation of plans into definite schedules usually occurs in series of interbureau conferences for which the Office of Land-Use Co-ordination acts as secretariat, preparing agendas and requested information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of interbureau conferences and representatives' responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences include representatives who are technical advisors and negotiators expected to criticize feasibility and indicate definitely what their bureaus are prepared to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representatives must consult with bureau chiefs and operating officials at stages; Office prepares minutes summarizing conclusions and outstanding issues; a schedule of operations is agreed upon, drafted by the Office and promulgated by the Secretary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-up planning (use and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans formulated by county and state representatives and checked by field experts and Washington technicians produce plans 'as good as could be made' but take a long time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bottom-up planning is based on first-hand experience and coordination but has long transit and review times (months), so is unsuitable when plans are needed quickly for emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-cut planning for emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When immediate action is required, planning begins in a central bureau which keeps essential work within its own hands to control the time element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bureau of Agricultural Economics sent investigators in 1938 to handle hurricane timber clearing. Short-cut planning avoids waiting on other units; except in extreme haste, interbureau programs are cleared through central coordinating offices to ascertain acceptance and agreement as to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust planning steps to relative importance of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and kind of steps in planning should be adjusted in each case to the relative importance of speed, technical accuracy, acceptability, and co-ordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must weigh trade-offs (speed vs accuracy/acceptability) and choose planning machinery appropriate to circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of management planning and administrative planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Management planning (larger administrative problems) and detailed administrative planning (regulations/procedures) can be separated; Departments have Divisions (Organization, Fiscal Management) and administrative councils to review and improve operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent changes show greater departmental interest in improving bureau organization and procedure; Division of Organization reviews organization plans; Division of Fiscal Management simplifies business procedures; an administrative council arbitrates management problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planners must have ability, authority, and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Good planning requires people within the organization who have the ability to plan, the authority to plan, and the time to plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line executives can plan if time is cleared by delegation or workload reduction; otherwise planning will be slow, inadequate, or omitted, or routine work will pile up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrating planning with line administration (Biological Survey example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning need not be separated from line administration; consistent delegation and assignment of detailed studies to line officials can permit planning without special planning officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chief called conferences to plan decentralization; business manager wrote a 'Regional Director's Manual' translating broad plans into working procedures; responsibility placed on line administrators to analyze new work and prepare combined administrative and management plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal planning appropriate only for small/simple agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal systems (individual line officials or occasional meetings) work in small, simple organizations but would cause confusion in large, complex ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success depends on wide delegation of routine work and absence of large fluctuating business; in large organizations absence of predetermined channels for planning is a source of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct management planning channels in large programs (Farm Security Administration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, multiple-activity programs require continuous and detailed administrative and executive planning with definite channels for each (e.g., Procedure Division, Instruction Manual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management planning centers in a Procedure Division which reviews and coordinates proposals of line officials, perfects routings and administrative steps, and maintains an Instruction Manual explaining organization and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal-stage content and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal is a simple preliminary plan showing whether cost of developing a complete plan is justified; contains social and economic data sufficient to show need and gross cost estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed estimates deferred until land optioned since physical characteristics affect costs; proposal prepared regionally with appropriate technicians simultaneously; reviewed by Washington technical sections for acceptance/modification/rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final plan content and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Final plan contains detailed justifying data, preliminary house plans, maps, specifications, and budget estimates for land purchase, construction, and administering the completed project; examined much more thoroughly than the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final plan developed for a specific tract and must be considered in relation to that land's characteristics; upon Administrator approval funds for optioning and purchases are authorized and acquisitions begin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-office technical review and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of offices participate in planning both proposal and final stages, each contributing specialized viewpoints; approved plans are checked for technical soundness and coordinated with the Administration's program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical sections review proposals from specialized points of view; Director of Resettlement Division evaluates in relation to program as a whole before Administrator decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central review justified when program lacks standard criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive scrutiny by central offices is warranted when a program is new, experimental, or lacks established standard criteria to avoid failure from social or economic planning mistakes or political pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During program expansion, projects were largely experiments and Administrator couldn't risk decentralizing authority until policies, criteria, and field training allowed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive decentralization as policies and criteria develop
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for execution should be decentralized as fast as development of policies, criteria, and training of field officials permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washington office would confine itself to program/policy planning, broad-scale supervision, inspection, and analysis; increasing field participation in planning and standard operating practice development prepares regions to take responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master plans, priorities, and workload analysis (Forest Service model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating divisions prepare master plans establishing project priorities; funds allotted according to priorities; annual work-load analyses classify tasks by function and organizational unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work-load analyses divided into Section I (recurrent work) and Section II (non-recurrent work such as construction, surveys, and special projects); analyses initiated in Ranger Districts and National Forest offices and reviewed regionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boards of Review and counterbalancing undue pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional Boards of Review with a regional planning officer as executive secretary counterbalance undue pressures from operating divisions and exercise coordination and determination of essential priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries of present workload and project work are forwarded to Washington in time for annual budget preparation (arrive before April 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning procedure and administrative urgency trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Subdivision of planning into many steps increases completion time; concentrating planning in a single unit may reduce soundness and acceptability; administrators must judge between these evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of planning must fit circumstances; if plans needed quickly, concentrate planning in a central office with immediate access to units; if time permits, spread planning with a central coordinating body to improve accuracy and acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of schedules to speed complex planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex planning procedures can be speeded up by setting and maintaining a schedule of operations; ample planning time is preferable to hurried planning that leads to waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough planning permits greater decentralization, fewer control steps, and less administrative delay; spending time in planning saves time and money in execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of procedural side of staff functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural aspects of staff functions (purchasing, personnel, legal, fiscal) are vital because effects of good or bad procedure are felt outside the staff unit; operations must happen at the right time and in the right way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff specialists must attend to how business comes to them, internal administrative sequences, and return channels to line officers; avoiding administrative motion delay is critical to efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient stock requisition procedure (Agency A model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct requisition to the warehouse with minimal moves and control steps allows rapid supply delivery; responsibility lies with the official who signs the requisition to ensure right kind and budget conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency A: requisition signed and sent directly to warehouse, received by Accounting Clerk who checks prices, credits warehouse, debits ordering office, sends copy to supply room and to Finance for entry — only two moves and one control step before forwarding supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inefficient stock requisition anti-pattern (Agency B model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple copies, divisional supply officers, pre-audits, and centralized mail distribution increase motion delay, divide responsibility, and cause confusion and 'buck-passing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency B: five copies, supply officer checks prices, forwards to division chief who signs, Finance pre-audits and encumbers funds, inter-divisional mail routing causes delays; results in uncertainty about responsibility and delays up to two days or more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single clear responsibility for orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether responsibility rests with ordering official or stock manager is less important than that it be given wholly and unquestionably to one individual, with direct communication between parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning clear responsibility eliminates confusion, delay, and buck-passing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision factors for open market vs centralized/branch purchasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must decide how centralized purchasing should be, whether branch purchasing offices should serve line divisions or geographic units, how flexible policies will be, and to what extent purchasing may occur outside regular channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scattered organizations often allow branches leeway to buy for immediate needs; the degree of leeway ranges from broad permission to narrow emergency-only purchasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field units' direct purchase limits tied to advertising laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Leeway for direct purchases by minor field units is generally based on the size of purchase which may lawfully be made without advertising for bids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In government, limits for direct purchases often reflect legal thresholds; concept of 'emergency' purchases has been narrowly defined (floods, fires, accidents, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and advantages of term contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Term contracts have contractors supply at a fixed unit price as many items as needed over a definite period; combine procedural advantage of direct purchasing with economic benefit of centralized buying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best service when contractor has suitably located sales branches or dealers for immediate delivery; Procurement Division negotiates such contracts for government use.
